30:48.en: Allah is He Who sendeth the winds so that they raise clouds, and spreadeth them along the sky as pleaseth Him, and causeth them to break and thou seest the rain downpouring from within them. And when He maketh it to fall on whom He will of His bondmen, lo! they rejoice

30:49.ar: وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلِ أَن يُنَزَّلَ عَلَيۡهِم مِّن قَبۡلِهِۦ لَمُبۡلِسِينَ

30:50.ar: فَٱنظُرۡ إِلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِ رَحۡمَتِ ٱللَّهِ كَيۡفَ يُحۡيِ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ بَعۡدَ مَوۡتِهَآۚ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ لَمُحۡيِ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰۖ وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيۡءࣲ قَدِيرࣱ‏

31:15.ar: وَإِن جَٰهَدَاكَ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تُشۡرِكَ بِي مَا لَيۡسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلۡمࣱ فَلَا تُطِعۡهُمَاۖ وَصَاحِبۡهُمَا فِي ٱلدُّنۡيَا مَعۡرُوفࣰ اۖ وَٱتَّبِعۡ سَبِيلَ مَنۡ أَنَابَ إِلَيَّۚ ثُمَّ إِلَيَّ مَرۡجِعُكُمۡ فَأُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
31:15.en: But if they strive with thee to make thee ascribe unto Me as partner that of which thou hast no knowledge, then obey them not. sysfOtpn8jo.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 20: Divine Hypotheses
sysfOtpn8jo.one_line: Only Allah can say what would have happened: three Quranic 'ifs' about fragile faith, hostile parents and the companions at the Trench.
sysfOtpn8jo.summary: He opens by warning that human 'what ifs' about the past and future are harmful: replaying missed chances traps people in a single moment, and endless future possibilities breed anxiety. We must plan for the likely and learn from mistakes, but only Allah, who knows what did not happen and how it would have unfolded, can state such hypotheses. Our current state is a product of circumstances that conceal our weaknesses, so we should be humble, ask for wellbeing and use our present leeway to grow. From 30:48-51 he shows people rejoicing at rain after despair, and Allah stating that had He sent a wind they saw as yellow they would have reverted to disbelief: faith that depends on getting what you want is fragile. From 31:14-15 he notes that even parents who strive to pull you from your faith are owed kind companionship, as some converts in his city live in reality, so ordinary Muslims owe their parents far more. Finally, 33:14, his most frightening verse, tells the companions at the Trench that had Madinah been overrun they would have given up their faith with little hesitation. He asks each listener to find his own breaking point and work to push it further away.

outline.heading: 'What if' about the past and future harms you
outline.gist: Replaying what could have been tears you apart, and trying to account for every future possibility has no end and can make you ill.

outline.heading: Plan and learn, but do not live in hypotheticals
outline.gist: You must plan for common variables and identify past mistakes to repent from them; take the lesson, keep the remorse and move on.

outline.heading: Only Allah can state what would have happened
outline.gist: His knowledge covers what did not occur and how it would have unfolded; no one else can say 'had I gone a day earlier I would have got the job'.

outline.heading: 'If' opens the door to Shaytan
outline.gist: The Prophet forbade it because Shaytan uses it to berate you; he knows people stuck for years in one moment of loss.

outline.heading: Your circumstances conceal your weaknesses
outline.gist: None of us knows who we would be had we been dealt a different hand; a few changes would expose our shortcomings, which is why we ask Allah for wellbeing and stay humble.

outline.heading: Allah knows your breaking point: use the leeway now
outline.gist: Remembering this makes you grateful and cautious; work on weaknesses while you have time, before life throws you into survival mode.

outline.heading: Winds, clouds and rain as mercy
outline.gist: Rain brings hope of a good year; living by the Great Lakes, people forget its value and even complain about it.

outline.heading: Despair before the rain and the name Iblis
outline.gist: Just before it rained they were 'mublisin', without hope, the same root as Iblis, who lost all hope of Allah's mercy.

outline.heading: The traces of mercy and the resurrection
outline.gist: Look how Allah revives dead land; the same process will bring the dead out of their graves.

outline.heading: 'Had We sent a wind and they saw it yellow'
outline.gist: Rain winds are cool and blue, sand winds yellow; had the wind brought sand they would have persisted in disbelief.

outline.heading: Circumstantial iman is fragile
outline.gist: Faith built on getting what you want collapses with a small shift; scholars note the verse says they merely saw it as yellow, even if it carried rain.

outline.heading: The dramatic human being, except those who pray
outline.gist: Disbelief here can also mean ingratitude; humans despair at hardship and hoard good, except those who truly understand prayer.

outline.heading: Iman the winds of life cannot shake
outline.gist: Whether the winds are blue or yellow, keep hope, gratitude and the memory of resurrection.

outline.heading: Weakness upon weakness: gratitude to Allah and parents
outline.gist: Pregnancy is so fragile that its success is remarkable; Allah commands gratitude to Him and to one's parents.

outline.heading: If they strive to make you associate, do not obey
outline.gist: A rare hypothetical: parents fighting with all their might to pull you from your faith are not obeyed in that.

outline.heading: Yet remain their kind companion
outline.gist: Anyone else attacking your faith you would leave; parents doing so must still be accompanied with the best of conduct.

outline.heading: For converts it is not hypothetical
outline.gist: Most Muslims' parents are proud of their faith, but several local converts face parents actively working against it; if they owe kindness, what do you owe your parents?

outline.heading: His most frightening verse and the hardest day
outline.gist: From his personal ranking of verses, this is the scariest; the Trench was by far the community's hardest moment, with 10,000 marching on Madinah.

outline.heading: The Confederates and the trench
outline.gist: Fifteen tribes, some hostile to each other, were kept apart on the march; the Muslims dug a five-kilometre trench in about two weeks.

outline.heading: Madinah's terrain and the northern fortresses
outline.gist: Lava fields east and west are impassable, as he learned dropping a rock into a crater there with his father's friend; fortresses guarded the north, leaving only the south open.

outline.heading: The plot to open the north and the Muslims' fear
outline.gist: Quraysh struck a deal with the owners of the northern fortresses; terror spread and some left their posts along the thinly guarded trench.

outline.heading: The wind that broke the siege
outline.gist: The deal collapsed and a ferocious wind tore the Confederates' tents, ending Quraysh's last attempt to harm the Muslims.

outline.heading: 'Had it been entered from all sides': they would have given in
outline.gist: Had the city fallen and they been asked at swordpoint to renounce Islam, some present would have done so after only brief hesitation.

outline.heading: Only Allah could say this of the companions
outline.gist: Were he to say it he would be thrown out of the masjid; Allah says it because He sees who they would have been had circumstances changed.

outline.heading: No names, so each could strengthen himself
outline.gist: The aim was not to shame them but to let each find the weakness in his iman and change the hypothesis.

outline.heading: Do you know your breaking point?
outline.gist: Not working to push your breaking point away is a kind of arrogance before Allah; be grateful that He has spared you the circumstances that would have broken you.

39:42.ar: ٱللَّهُ يَتَوَفَّى ٱلۡأَنفُسَ حِينَ مَوۡتِهَا وَٱلَّتِي لَمۡ تَمُتۡ فِي مَنَامِهَاۖ فَيُمۡسِكُ ٱلَّتِي قَضَىٰ عَلَيۡهَا ٱلۡمَوۡتَ وَيُرۡسِلُ ٱلۡأُخۡرَىٰٓ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلࣲ مُّسَمًّىۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّقَوۡمࣲ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ
39:42.en: Allah receiveth (men's) souls at the time of their death, and that (soul) which dieth not (yet) in its sleep. He keepeth that (soul) for which He hath ordained death and dismisseth the rest till an appointed term. Lo! herein verily are portents for people who take thought

7:20.ar: فَوَسۡوَسَ لَهُمَا ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ لِيُبۡدِيَ لَهُمَا مَا وُۥرِيَ عَنۡهُمَا مِن سَوۡءَٰتِهِمَا وَقَالَ مَا نَهَىٰكُمَا رَبُّكُمَا عَنۡ هَٰذِهِ ٱلشَّجَرَةِ إِلَّآ أَن تَكُونَا مَلَكَيۡنِ أَوۡ تَكُونَا مِنَ ٱلۡخَٰلِدِينَ

7:21.en: And he swore unto them (saying): Lo! I am a sincere adviser unto you

7GQT-LdoLBg.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 13: Accepting Mortality
7GQT-LdoLBg.one_line: Accepting mortality, not obsessing over death, as the strongest tool for taming the self, possible only when death is seen as a transition.
7GQT-LdoLBg.summary: He distinguishes the moment of death, which is unknown and not worth obsessing over, from mortality, the fact that you will not exist here forever. It is the self, not the soul, that dreads death, because it exists only while soul and body are joined. He reads Adam's slip as driven by fear of death: Iblis promised immortality, and the one caveat in an otherwise perfect package was the part Adam wanted removed. Muslims, he finds from his clinical work, have lost the maturity they once had about death, and the Prophet's warning of a numerous but weightless ummah describes love of this world and hatred of death driving every decision. Immortality would kill motivation; finitude is what makes time precious. Because the self fears death above all, accepting mortality is the ultimate leverage over it. Yet nobody can accept death as an end into nothingness; peace comes only when death is seen as a transition to the barzakh and resurrection, which replaces a paralysing fear with a productive fear of judgment. Acceptance passes through grief, and he describes elderly patients who still felt they had not lived. The self's lie is that you have plenty of time; the truth is that life can end without warning. He asks listeners to live so that knowing they would die tomorrow would change nothing.

outline.heading: Mortality, not the moment of death
outline.gist: Obsessing over when or how you will die is useless; contemplate the fact that you will not live forever.

outline.heading: The two primal fears: death and pain
outline.gist: The soul returns to Allah in sleep and does not fear death; the self fears death, and both fear suffering.

outline.heading: Why the self fears death
outline.gist: The self exists only while soul and body are joined, so it sees death as its end until resurrection restores both.

outline.heading: Adam's garden: safety, provision and companionship
outline.gist: Read symbolically, the garden gave Adam everything he needed, so why would he touch the one forbidden thing?

outline.heading: Iblis's promise of immortality
outline.gist: Iblis claimed the tree would make him an angel or immortal; Adam loved the package but not its caveat of death, and fear of death drove the slip.

outline.heading: Adam as the raw, untamed self
outline.gist: Adam was meeting his urges and instincts for the first time, before he could break them down.

outline.heading: Muslims have lost their maturity about death
outline.gist: From his clinical work he sees some atheists accept mortality better than Muslims, for whom it should be natural.

outline.heading: Love of this world and hatred of death
outline.gist: In the hadith of nations devouring a numerous but weightless ummah, neither feeling is wrong in itself; the problem is when they drive every decision.

outline.heading: Those who would live a thousand years
outline.gist: The Quran describes people who cling to any life at any price, which will not save them.

outline.heading: Immortality stories always bring death back
outline.gist: Authors who pursue immortal societies end with people choosing death again, since we need endings.

outline.heading: Endless time kills motivation
outline.gist: If you lived forever, everything could wait until tomorrow and nothing would get done.

outline.heading: Finitude makes life precious
outline.gist: Mortality is meant to bring joy, not depression; scarce time is valued and appreciated.

outline.heading: Mortality: the ultimate weapon against the self
outline.gist: Death is what the self fears most; once you no longer fear it, reminding the self of death makes it retreat.

outline.heading: Why simulating death fails
outline.gist: His long courses of death contemplation failed while people saw death as nothingness, which no one can accept.

outline.heading: Peace only through seeing death as a transition
outline.gist: Death is a move from one mode of existence to the next, through resurrection to the final abode.

outline.heading: Clarity on the barzakh and resurrection
outline.gist: The barzakh is the transitional space; certainty about resurrection is the second requirement for accepting mortality.

outline.heading: From fearing nothingness to a productive fear of judgment
outline.gist: With certainty, the fear becomes whether you did enough, a fear that motivates rather than depresses.

outline.heading: The stages of grief on the way to acceptance
outline.gist: Denial, depression, anxiety and anger are natural steps in contemplating your mortality.

outline.heading: Healthy sadness, fear for loved ones, and a written will
outline.gist: Sadness at losing life's blessing is natural; fear of darkness signals weak faith; putting affairs in order eases the transition.

outline.heading: The eighty-year-old who had not lived yet
outline.gist: A patient with two spreading cancers on oxygen demanded a cure because he had not lived; without accepting mortality, no age feels enough.

outline.heading: Living in extra time
outline.gist: Scholars lived as if the ninety minutes were over, grateful for each added minute.

outline.heading: The self's lie and the patient hoping for another year
outline.gist: A man in his nineties kept hoping for one or two more years, endlessly.

outline.heading: Mortality beautifies every moment
outline.gist: With days left, every breath, breeze, cup of water and conversation becomes precious.

outline.heading: The last-week exercise and why it fades
outline.gist: Living a week as your last works for a day or two because it is also a lie, but so is believing you have plenty of time.

outline.heading: Procrastination: the enemy of mortality
outline.gist: Putting off what matters assumes a date you cannot guarantee.

outline.heading: The truth: it can end at any moment
outline.gist: Hope for a long life, but live by the real possibility that it ends without warning.

outline.heading: Acceptance liberates, as with the Prophet
outline.gist: He neither sought nor feared death and met it ready; accepting mortality frees you from enslavement to anything but Allah.

outline.heading: Why we are not told when we will die
outline.gist: Patients given three months make decisions they never could, because the frightened self falls quiet.

outline.heading: If you died tomorrow, what would you change?
outline.gist: Whatever you would change, change now; if you would quit work or school, ask why you were doing it.

outline.heading: Without accepting mortality, nothing else works
outline.gist: As long as you believe you have plenty of time, Islam stays foreign and difficult to practise.

outline.heading: Outro

24:63.ar: لَّا تَجۡعَلُواْ دُعَآءَ ٱلرَّسُولِ بَيۡنَكُمۡ كَدُعَآءِ بَعۡضِكُم بَعۡضࣰ اۚ قَدۡ يَعۡلَمُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَتَسَلَّلُونَ مِنكُمۡ لِوَاذࣰ اۚ فَلۡيَحۡذَرِ ٱلَّذِينَ يُخَالِفُونَ عَنۡ أَمۡرِهِۦٓ أَن تُصِيبَهُمۡ فِتۡنَةٌ أَوۡ يُصِيبَهُمۡ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ
24:63.en: Make not the calling of the messenger among you as your calling one of another. Allah knoweth those of you who steal away, hiding themselves. And let those who conspire to evade orders beware lest grief or painful punishment befall them

2:67.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوۡمِهِۦٓ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأۡمُرُكُمۡ أَن تَذۡبَحُواْ بَقَرَةࣰۖ قَالُوٓاْ أَتَتَّخِذُنَا هُزُوࣰ اۖ قَالَ أَعُوذُ بِٱللَّهِ أَنۡ أَكُونَ مِنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
2:67.en: And when Moses said unto his people: Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye sacrifice a cow, they said: Dost thou make game of us? He answered: Allah forbid that I should be among the foolish

2:68.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ لَّا فَارِضࣱ وَلَا بِكۡرٌ عَوَانُۢ بَيۡنَ ذَٰلِكَۖ فَٱفۡعَلُواْ مَا تُؤۡمَرُونَ
2:68.en: They said: Pray for us unto thy Lord that He make clear to us what (cow) she is. (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith, Verily she is a cow neither with calf nor immature; (she is) between the two conditions; so do that which ye are commanded

2:69.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا لَوۡنُهَاۚ قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ صَفۡرَآءُ فَاقِعࣱ لَّوۡنُهَا تَسُرُّ ٱلنَّٰظِرِينَ
2:69.en: They said: Pray for us unto thy Lord that He make clear to us of what colour she is. (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith: Verily she is a yellow cow. Bright is her colour, gladdening beholders

2:70.ar: قَالُواْ ٱدۡعُ لَنَا رَبَّكَ يُبَيِّن لَّنَا مَا هِيَ إِنَّ ٱلۡبَقَرَ تَشَٰبَهَ عَلَيۡنَا وَإِنَّآ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَمُهۡتَدُونَ
2:70.en: They said: Pray for us unto thy Lord that He make clear to us what (cow) she is. Lo! cows are much alike to us; and Lo! if Allah wills, we may be led aright

2:71.ar: قَالَ إِنَّهُۥ يَقُولُ إِنَّهَا بَقَرَةࣱ لَّا ذَلُولࣱ تُثِيرُ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ وَلَا تَسۡقِي ٱلۡحَرۡثَ مُسَلَّمَةࣱ لَّا شِيَةَ فِيهَاۚ قَالُواْ ٱلۡـَٰٔنَ جِئۡتَ بِٱلۡحَقِّۚ فَذَبَحُوهَا وَمَا كَادُواْ يَفۡعَلُونَ
2:71.en: (Moses) answered: Lo! He saith: Verily she is a cow unyoked; she plougheth not the soil nor watereth the tilth; whole and without mark. They said: Now thou bringest the truth. So they sacrificed her, though almost they did not

cHua9xyaJgQ.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 12: Haya and Etiquette
cHua9xyaJgQ.one_line: Haya redefined as awareness and sensitivity, the uncapped ethic that generates all others and produces adab, the key to receiving from Allah.
cHua9xyaJgQ.summary: He presents haya as the ethic that represents Islam and argues it is not shyness, introversion or bashfulness. Its root is life itself: haya is the peak of being alive, which means being aware of yourself and others and sensitive to their needs, as a child should notice an elder needs water. Without it, as ancient prophetic wisdom says, you will do anything. Haya generates the other virtues, compassion and humbleness among them, and unlike every other ethic it needs no cap. It is not passive aggression or bottled anger, which he sees as rife in Canadian society. Reducing haya to dress code butchers it; modest dress is only one expression of awareness of how you affect others. Haya's fruit is adab, the door through which Allah gives knowledge and acceptance. He cites the Prophet's manners, the verses on lowering voices before him, and scholars who spent far longer learning a teacher's adab than his knowledge. Adab governs how we make dua, how we approach people, and whether we can disagree without fracturing, since Islam was designed to hold many views. Sensitivity also shows in how many of our own sins we can name. He ends with companions too reverent to gaze at the Prophet, and insists adab reflects who you are, so it cannot be selective.

outline.heading: Haya: the ethic that represents Islam
outline.gist: Every faith has a defining character, and Islam's is haya.

outline.heading: Haya as a branch of faith
outline.gist: Faith has many levels, from its highest truth to removing harm from the road, and haya is singled out as its own branch.

outline.heading: Haya is not shyness
outline.gist: It is not shame, bashfulness or introversion, even if it often shows as a lowered voice.

outline.heading: Awareness plus sensitivity: the elder who needs water
outline.gist: A child who does not notice an elder is thirsty or needs a tissue lacks the awareness and sensitivity that make up haya.

outline.heading: Haya as the peak of being alive
outline.gist: The word comes from the root of life; the dead neither notice nor respond, so someone without awareness and sensitivity barely exists in their world.

outline.heading: Without haya you will do anything
outline.gist: Ancient prophetic wisdom: if you feel no shame, do as you wish, since nothing regulates you.

outline.heading: Haya generates every other ethic
outline.gist: Awareness and sensitivity produce compassion and make arrogance impossible.

outline.heading: The one ethic with no cap
outline.gist: Mercy and humbleness need regulating; haya only brings good, so the more the better.

outline.heading: Haya is not bottled-up resentment
outline.gist: Polite words carrying hidden jabs, or suppressed anger, are not haya but social regulation.

outline.heading: Passive aggression versus honest anger
outline.gist: He sees passive aggression as extreme in Canada and prefers even loud Middle Eastern honesty, because at least you know where you stand.

outline.heading: The person of haya is always scanning
outline.gist: They know where they stand with people, place and time, and respond to how they affect others.

outline.heading: Haya reduced to dress code
outline.gist: Modest dress is one valid expression of awareness of how one's appearance affects society, but reducing haya to it butchers the ethic.

outline.heading: Haya produces adab, the door to Allah's giving
outline.gist: Without etiquette every door of knowledge and acceptance from Allah stays closed.

outline.heading: The Prophet's adab at doors and with food
outline.gist: He stood to the side of doors rather than facing in, and never criticised food: he ate it or left it.

outline.heading: Raising voices over the Prophet erases deeds
outline.gist: Good manners are part of prophecy; the verses on lowering voices show lack of adab can wipe out the reward of good deeds.

outline.heading: Learning a teacher's adab before his knowledge
outline.gist: Malik's mother told him to learn his teacher's adab first; a student of Malik spent most of twenty years learning his adab.

outline.heading: A little adab over much knowledge
outline.gist: Knowledge does not benefit without adab; a scholar was rebuked by an elderly woman for stretching his foot in a gathering of knowledge.

outline.heading: Scholars preferred stories of the righteous
outline.gist: Early scholars valued accounts of how the pious lived, and discussed etiquette more than rulings.

outline.heading: Adab with Allah in dua
outline.gist: Knowing how to address Allah takes learning; if unsure, use the words of the Quran.

outline.heading: Adab in asking people for help
outline.gist: People want to help those who ask with respect; he describes the angry, demanding messages he sometimes receives.

outline.heading: Adab opens doors with people
outline.gist: Courtesy makes people like and serve you; its absence turns differences into rifts.

outline.heading: Adab lets us disagree: Islam's diversity is by design
outline.gist: Islam is a wide river with many lanes; as with the cow of Bani Isra'il, many options would have been acceptable.

outline.heading: The exercise: name fifty separate sins
outline.gist: Most people stall at twenty, not for lack of sins but for lack of sensitivity.

outline.heading: Sensitivity changes what counts as a shortcoming
outline.gist: What we count as a good day, such as praying Fajr barely on time, the Prophet would count as cause for repentance.

outline.heading: Leaving what does not concern you
outline.gist: The easygoing and gentle are praised; part of good Islam is knowing what to stay out of.

outline.heading: Why descriptions of the Prophet come from children
outline.gist: Adult companions were too reverent to stare at his face; they sat as if a bird were perched on their heads.

outline.heading: Adab reflects you, so it cannot be selective
outline.gist: You respect people because you are respectful, not because they are; selective adab is a preference, not a value.

28:22.ar: وَلَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ تِلۡقَآءَ مَدۡيَنَ قَالَ عَسَىٰ رَبِّيٓ أَن يَهۡدِيَنِي سَوَآءَ ٱلسَّبِيلِ
28:22.en: And when he turned his face toward Midian, he said: Peradventure my Lord will guide me in the right road

28:23.ar: وَلَمَّا وَرَدَ مَآءَ مَدۡيَنَ وَجَدَ عَلَيۡهِ أُمَّةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلنَّاسِ يَسۡقُونَ وَوَجَدَ مِن دُونِهِمُ ٱمۡرَأَتَيۡنِ تَذُودَانِۖ قَالَ مَا خَطۡبُكُمَاۖ قَالَتَا لَا نَسۡقِي حَتَّىٰ يُصۡدِرَ ٱلرِّعَآءُۖ وَأَبُونَا شَيۡخࣱ كَبِيرࣱ‏
28:23.en: And when he came unto the water of Midian he found there a whole tribe of men, watering. And he found apart from them two women keeping back (their flocks). He said: What aileth you? The two said: We cannot give (our flocks) to drink till the shepherds return from the water; and our father is a very old man

28:24.ar: فَسَقَىٰ لَهُمَا ثُمَّ تَوَلَّىٰٓ إِلَى ٱلظِّلِّ فَقَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي لِمَآ أَنزَلۡتَ إِلَيَّ مِنۡ خَيۡرࣲ فَقِيرࣱ‏
28:24.en: So he watered (their flock) for them. Then he turned aside into the shade, and said: My Lord! I am needy of whatever good Thou sendest down for me

28:25.ar: فَجَآءَتۡهُ إِحۡدَىٰهُمَا تَمۡشِي عَلَى ٱسۡتِحۡيَآءࣲ قَالَتۡ إِنَّ أَبِي يَدۡعُوكَ لِيَجۡزِيَكَ أَجۡرَ مَا سَقَيۡتَ لَنَاۚ فَلَمَّا جَآءَهُۥ وَقَصَّ عَلَيۡهِ ٱلۡقَصَصَ قَالَ لَا تَخَفۡۖ نَجَوۡتَ مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
28:25.en: Then there came unto him one of the two women, walking shyly. She said: Lo! my father biddeth thee, that he may reward thee with a payment for that thou didst water (the flock) for us. Then, when he came unto him and told him the (whole) story, he said: Fear not! Thou hast escaped from the wrongdoing folk

28:26.ar: قَالَتۡ إِحۡدَىٰهُمَا يَٰٓأَبَتِ ٱسۡتَـٔۡجِرۡهُۖ إِنَّ خَيۡرَ مَنِ ٱسۡتَـٔۡجَرۡتَ ٱلۡقَوِيُّ ٱلۡأَمِينُ
28:26.en: One of the two women said: O my father! Hire him! For the best (man) that thou canst hire in the strong, the trustworthy

28:27.ar: قَالَ إِنِّيٓ أُرِيدُ أَنۡ أُنكِحَكَ إِحۡدَى ٱبۡنَتَيَّ هَٰتَيۡنِ عَلَىٰٓ أَن تَأۡجُرَنِي ثَمَٰنِيَ حِجَجࣲۖ فَإِنۡ أَتۡمَمۡتَ عَشۡرࣰ ا فَمِنۡ عِندِكَۖ وَمَآ أُرِيدُ أَنۡ أَشُقَّ عَلَيۡكَۚ سَتَجِدُنِيٓ إِن شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ مِنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
28:27.en: He said: Lo! I fain would marry thee to one of these two daughters of mine on condition that thou hirest thyself to me for (the term of) eight pilgrimages. Then if thou completest ten it will be of thine own accord, for I would not make it hard for thee. Allah willing, thou wilt find me of the righteous

28:44.ar: وَمَا كُنتَ بِجَانِبِ ٱلۡغَرۡبِيِّ إِذۡ قَضَيۡنَآ إِلَىٰ مُوسَى ٱلۡأَمۡرَ وَمَا كُنتَ مِنَ ٱلشَّٰهِدِينَ
28:44.en: And thou (Muhammad) wast not on the western side (of the Mount) when We expounded unto Moses the commandment, and thou wast not among those present

28:45.ar: وَلَٰكِنَّآ أَنشَأۡنَا قُرُونࣰ ا فَتَطَاوَلَ عَلَيۡهِمُ ٱلۡعُمُرُۚ وَمَا كُنتَ ثَاوِيࣰ ا فِيٓ أَهۡلِ مَدۡيَنَ تَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِنَا وَلَٰكِنَّا كُنَّا مُرۡسِلِينَ
28:45.en: But We brought forth generations, and their lives dragged on for them. And thou wast not a dweller in Midian, reciting unto them Our revelations, but We kept sending (messengers to men)

28:46.ar: وَمَا كُنتَ بِجَانِبِ ٱلطُّورِ إِذۡ نَادَيۡنَا وَلَٰكِن رَّحۡمَةࣰ مِّن رَّبِّكَ لِتُنذِرَ قَوۡمࣰ ا مَّآ أَتَىٰهُم مِّن نَّذِيرࣲ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ
28:46.en: And thou was not beside the Mount when We did call; but (the knowledge of it is) a mercy from thy Lord that thou mayst warn a folk unto whom no warner came before thee, that haply they may give heed

29:2.ar: أَحَسِبَ ٱلنَّاسُ أَن يُتۡرَكُوٓاْ أَن يَقُولُوٓاْ ءَامَنَّا وَهُمۡ لَا يُفۡتَنُونَ
29:2.en: Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction

29:3.ar: وَلَقَدۡ فَتَنَّا ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِهِمۡۖ فَلَيَعۡلَمَنَّ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ صَدَقُواْ وَلَيَعۡلَمَنَّ ٱلۡكَٰذِبِينَ
29:3.en: Lo! We tested those who were before you. Thus Allah knoweth those who are sincere, and knoweth those who feign

20:17.en: And what is that in thy right hand, O Moses

20:18.ar: قَالَ هِيَ عَصَايَ أَتَوَكَّؤُاْ عَلَيۡهَا وَأَهُشُّ بِهَا عَلَىٰ غَنَمِي وَلِيَ فِيهَا مَـَٔارِبُ أُخۡرَىٰ
20:18.en: He said: This is my staff whereon I lean, and wherewith I bear down branches for my sheep, and wherein I find other uses

20:19.en: He said: Cast it down, O Moses

20:20.en: So he cast it down, and lo! it was a serpent, gliding

20:21.ar: قَالَ خُذۡهَا وَلَا تَخَفۡۖ سَنُعِيدُهَا سِيرَتَهَا ٱلۡأُولَىٰ
20:21.en: He said: Grasp it and fear not. We shall return it to its former state

8hlAROz9ZjA.speaker_note: Ramadan Quranic Themes series on his channel; refers back to his own earlier nights in the series
8hlAROz9ZjA.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 19: Understanding Relationships
8hlAROz9ZjA.one_line: Three Quranic lessons on relationships: see people's essence as the old man of Madyan saw Musa, do not judge what you did not witness, and expect life to test you.
8hlAROz9ZjA.summary: He argues that relationships, like having a worldview, cannot be avoided: you relate to people, time and hardship whether you mean to or not, and the maturity of those relationships shapes how functional and fulfilled you are. The Quran teaches this through examples, and Ramadan is the time to review them. From the story of Musa in Madyan he shows an old man offering his daughter in marriage to a starving, homeless stranger because he saw character and potential rather than wealth or status, and he uses this to condemn a community that makes halal marriage costly and slow while haram is everywhere, leaving young people to age without families. From 28:44-46, where Allah tells the Prophet he was not present for Musa's experiences, he draws that we should not judge people for situations we never lived, supporting it with al-Miqdad's rebuke of a man who wished he had seen the Prophet and Hudhayfah's account of the night of the Trench; understanding is not justifying wrong. From 29:2-3 he teaches that one's relationship with the future must assume continual testing in ease and hardship, met with striving, patience and realistic expectations rather than shielded entitlement.

outline.heading: Relationships as a Quranic theme
outline.gist: Distinct from the relationship with Allah: how we relate to people, the world, time and difficulty.

outline.heading: You cannot opt out of relationships
outline.gist: Just as everyone has a religion, even agnosticism, and every living person communicates somehow, every person has relationships that will be defined one way or another.

outline.heading: The Quran teaches relationships by example
outline.gist: Rather than naming attitudes, it shows interactions between spouses, friends, prophets and followers; the more mature your relationships, the more functional and fulfilled you are.

outline.heading: Ramadan as a time to review your relationships
outline.gist: Step back to consider your relationship and obligations toward parents, spouse, siblings, children, community, time and environment.

outline.heading: Musa flees Egypt and reaches Madyan
outline.gist: Pharaoh wanted a pretext to kill the justice-minded Musa; he fled on foot and arrived starving, barefoot and gaunt after eating leaves.

outline.heading: Musa waters the women's flock
outline.gist: Two young women held back their thirsty sheep to avoid the shepherds; with an aged father and no brother, Musa watered the flock for them and turned to Allah in need.

outline.heading: The modest invitation and Musa's account
outline.gist: One daughter came walking with modesty and had him walk ahead; he told the old man his story, holding knowledge from the remnants of Yusuf's teaching.

outline.heading: 'Hire him: the strong and the trustworthy'
outline.gist: The daughter noticed he did a favour without asking improper questions, staring or flirting, and was clearly capable.

outline.heading: The offer of marriage for eight years of work
outline.gist: The old man offered one of his daughters for eight years of shepherding, ten if Musa wished, promising to be easy on him.

outline.heading: No one else would have opened the door to Musa
outline.gist: With no job, home, money, family or language, every door would have closed; the wise old man saw his character and potential beyond the rags.

outline.heading: Making halal hard while haram is everywhere
outline.gist: With biting sarcasm he condemns costly, showy marriage processes that leave suitable young men and women unmarried into their thirties and push them down other paths.

outline.heading: What a suitor really needs
outline.gist: Telling a struggling 23-year-old to wait six years is unrealistic; he needs to be decent, hardworking, noble and trustworthy, not to hold every key. He calls the crisis a threat to the ummah and laments that marital obligations are no longer taught.

outline.heading: The old man won by seeing beyond the surface
outline.gist: His daughter became a prophet's wife and his grandchildren a prophet's sons; those who would have turned Musa away lost. Seeing people's worth is a skill.

outline.heading: 'You were not there': a unique address to the Prophet
outline.gist: Allah tells the Prophet he was not at the mountain, nor in Madyan, nor a witness, an address found nowhere else in the Quran.

outline.heading: Musa runs from the serpent: not yours to judge
outline.gist: Readers wonder why Musa fled when his staff became a serpent; the verses answer that you were not there to judge it.

outline.heading: Not judging is basic to every relationship
outline.gist: Alongside seeing people's essence, do not judge experiences you do not understand; take the message and warn people.

outline.heading: Musa's hesitations at the call
outline.gist: After the miracles Musa still worried about the man he had killed and his speech; we cannot say how we would have reacted.

outline.heading: Learn from stories without judging the people in them
outline.gist: Resolving not to repeat someone's mistake is good; condemning them because you think you would have done better is not.

outline.heading: Al-Miqdad and 'blessed are the eyes that saw him'
outline.gist: He rebuked a man for wishing he had seen the Prophet: you do not know how you would have behaved, and some who saw him ended in the Fire.

outline.heading: Hudhayfah and the night of the Trench
outline.gist: No one volunteered to scout despite the promise of Paradise; when a later listener boasted, Hudhayfah said you do not know the cold, hunger and fear we faced.

outline.heading: Only Allah is the judge; understanding is not justifying
outline.gist: Unless you are exempt from judgment yourself, hold back; the alternative to judging is understanding people's struggle, never justifying haram.

outline.heading: Even the Prophet is told not to question Musa
outline.gist: The Prophet might have longed for Musa's direct speech with Allah, yet he is told he was not there; Musa is not held to account by us.

outline.heading: The relationship with your future
outline.gist: After recapping the first two lessons, he turns to how we relate to time: the past is gone, but the future is a love-hate relationship of hope and dread.

outline.heading: 'Do people think they will be left alone?'
outline.gist: Declaring faith guarantees testing; life is a series of trials, some in wealth, health and success, some in disease and loss.

outline.heading: Every nation was tested; prophets most of all
outline.gist: Testing exposes the truthful and the liars, and the most tested are the prophets and then the most pious.

outline.heading: Prepare a cloak: life on the basis of striving
outline.gist: Expecting a red carpet makes every hardship a shock that tips you over; expecting challenge without pessimism keeps you steady.

outline.heading: Aces every hand makes a boring game
outline.gist: Friction is how we grow; ask Allah for ease and strength but walk out ready for whatever hand you are dealt.

outline.heading: See every gain and loss as a test
outline.gist: The job, the paycheque and the child are tests just as deprivation is; this puts you in step with the world.

outline.heading: Over-shielded children meet a harsh world
outline.gist: Parents who shield children from mistakes and accountability give them false expectations that the world corrects harshly. He closes by recapping the three relationships.

themes.label: Understanding relationships with people, time and life
themes.note: Relationships are unavoidable and their maturity decides how functional and fulfilled we are; the Quran teaches them through examples.

themes.label: Seeing people's worth beyond wealth and status
themes.note: The old man of Madyan saw Musa's character and potential where everyone else would have seen a destitute stranger.

themes.label: Marriage and the relationship between spouses
themes.note: The community makes marriage costly and slow while haram is easy, a real threat to the ummah; a suitor needs character, not every credential.

themes.label: Youth, their challenges and their role
themes.note: Young men told to wait years while struggling to stay chaste are being set up to fail.

themes.label: Withholding judgment of others
themes.note: You were not there, so do not judge; learn from others' stories and seek to understand without justifying wrong.

themes.label: Trials, hardship and resilience
themes.note: Faith guarantees testing in ease and hardship; realistic expectations keep you from being overturned by difficulty.

themes.label: Mujahadah: striving as a way of life
themes.note: The healthy relationship with life and the future is one of readiness to strive and persevere.

themes.label: Parenting and raising children
themes.note: Shielding children from mistakes and accountability leaves them unprepared for life.

LmIxqGPgHHs.title: Tafsir of Surat Al-Saffat, Part 5: Verses 75-98
LmIxqGPgHHs.one_line: Nuh obeys commands he cannot explain and learns there is no nepotism with Allah; Ibrahim's pure heart drives him to question and break the idols.
LmIxqGPgHHs.summary: He opens the stories section by restating the theme: obey Allah whether or not anyone can explain the wisdom, since every ruling serves an objective but obedience is not conditional on knowing it. In matters of the unseen we accept exactly what Allah said, add nothing, and do not draw analogies; what He left out, such as many names, He left out on purpose. Nuh's story is told briefly because almost everything in it resists explanation: 950 years of preaching, building a ship on a mountain far from water while being mocked as a carpenter, roughly eighty followers, and all later humanity descending from his line. He notes that the Quran does not say the flood was global, unlike the biblical account, whose text passed through languages and human hands. Nuh understood the command only when the flood came, and his heartbroken question about his drowned son earned the answer that there is no nepotism in this deen: lineage cannot carry a person whose deeds hold him back. Ibrahim's story begins with his pure heart, which the sheikh links to inner purification alongside outer cleanliness. That purity made him pursue truth over reputation and ask his people the essential question of what they think of the Lord of the worlds. He excused himself from their festival with a glance at the stars, broke the idols, and faced the fire, but Allah made his enemies the lowest.

outline.heading: Opening
Obey whether or not the wisdom is explained
outline.gist: Sometimes scholars can show the benefit of a command and sometimes not; either way Allah expects us to follow.

outline.heading: Every ruling serves an objective
outline.gist: No ruling exists for its own sake, and scholars study purposes, but knowing them is not the condition for obeying.

outline.heading: Accept the unseen as stated
outline.gist: The first seventy-four verses cannot be verified; we take them as Allah said them, adding and subtracting nothing.

outline.heading: No analogies in the unseen
outline.gist: Questions like whether angels marry have no basis and no benefit; we know only what Allah chose to tell.

outline.heading: What Allah left out, He left out on purpose
outline.gist: Many people in the Quran are unnamed because the name changes nothing; learn the point and avoid distraction.

outline.heading: Two trees in the surah
outline.gist: A tree to avoid in Hell and a tree hoped for later mirror each other, as Allah decrees.

outline.heading: Nuh's call after 950 years
outline.gist: The long story is compressed into a few lines because each prophet here received commands worth noting; Nuh called on Allah after centuries of rejection.

outline.heading: A ship on a mountain far from water
outline.gist: Nuh obeyed a command he could neither understand nor explain, reportedly planting trees to build it over decades.

outline.heading: Mocked as a carpenter; the best of responders
outline.gist: His people mocked his new profession; Allah praises Himself as the best responder to Nuh's call.

outline.heading: Saved from the great distress
outline.gist: Barely eighty believers in all that time, with his own wife and son refusing; still Allah saved him and those who followed.

outline.heading: His descendants alone remained
outline.gist: All humanity traces back to Nuh's line; why other survivors left no lineage no one knows.

outline.heading: Peace upon Nuh and the reward of excellence
outline.gist: He is honoured in every faith; Allah rewards those who did a hard job with excellence, and the rest drowned.

outline.heading: The flood was not necessarily global
outline.gist: The Quran says Nuh's people drowned, not the whole earth; the biblical text has passed through languages and human hands.

outline.heading: Where Nuh lived and was buried
outline.gist: The majority view places him between Mecca and Sham and his burial in Mecca.

outline.heading: The wisdom became clear in the flood
outline.gist: When the oven gushed water he boarded the believers, found animals lined up, sailed for months and settled on Judi.

outline.heading: Wisdom comes with time
outline.gist: We now know how much we do not know; answers arrive as we learn, so accept the command first.

outline.heading: Nuh's son and a heartbroken question
outline.gist: Promised his family's rescue, Nuh watched his son drown and asked, not objecting, why.

outline.heading: Nuh declines to intercede on Judgment Day
outline.gist: He will cite the question he should not have asked; Allah answered that the son was not of his family.

outline.heading: No nepotism in this deen
outline.gist: Even a prophet's son gets no special seat; lineage strengthens identity, but deeds, not ancestry, carry you.

outline.heading: Ibrahim of Nuh's party, with a sound heart
outline.gist: Shi'ah means followers and kin; Ibrahim's story is the main story of the surah, and his pure heart explains why he was chosen.

outline.heading: The sound heart on the Day of Resurrection
outline.gist: Ibrahim's own dua says wealth and children will not help, only a pure heart, the goal of the weekday tazkiyah sessions.

outline.heading: Purity outside and inside
outline.gist: Wudu and clean clothes mean little if the heart is arrogant, envious or insincere; Islam requires both, and most neglect the inner.

outline.heading: Everyone has a soul to refine
outline.gist: Even non-believers can reach some spirituality through reflection, though the real goal needs the Prophet's guidance.

outline.heading: Pursuing truth over reputation
outline.gist: Ibrahim worked on his heart from youth and cared nothing for popularity or safety, only truth, so he challenged his father's false gods.

outline.heading: 'What do you think of the Lord of the worlds?'
outline.gist: The essential question: a true understanding of Allah makes obedience second nature, while a made-up image of God lets people do as they please.

outline.heading: A glance at the stars and 'I am sick'
outline.gist: Pressed to join the idol festival, he looked up at the stars among astrologers, perhaps in despair at them, and excused himself so they left him behind.

outline.heading: Striking the idols
outline.gist: He went quietly to the idols, mocked them for neither eating nor speaking, and broke them with his right hand.

outline.heading: Why the story is summarised here
outline.gist: The Quran retells stories to focus on different parts; the details of the idols are elsewhere because this surah's point comes next.

outline.heading: You worship what you carve
outline.gist: They rushed at him; he asked why they worship their own handiwork when Allah created them and what they make.

outline.heading: A high structure, and the lowest outcome
outline.gist: They built a high pyre to burn him, so Allah made them the lowest.

KQXFx_vutvM.speaker_note: Tazkiyah Pearls series in his usual voice, continuing the Ramadan programme
KQXFx_vutvM.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 14: Tawakkul
KQXFx_vutvM.one_line: Tawakkul as the bridge between belief and action: full effort, dependence on Allah and contentment with His decree, and the freedom it brings.
KQXFx_vutvM.summary: He first explains why the series builds foundations like self-worth, compassion and mortality before any talk of spiritual states: emotional reminders without clear fundamentals give a short-lived high. Tawakkul links theology to practice, and it rests on the fact that we do not know what is best for us, as the Quran says and as a folk tale about a farmer's shifting fortunes shows. Nothing arrives labelled as blessing or punishment; we label it by how we respond, and no one can declare a hardship to be Allah's wrath. Hardships met with patience are tax-free, while blessings carry a debt of gratitude. After separating what you can control from what you cannot, he defines three components: doing your genuine best, without which tawakkul becomes a numbing excuse for passivity; depending on Allah for the outcome, since there are endless ways to fail even when prepared; and contentment with His decree, never with your own effort, expressed as gratitude in ease and perseverance in hardship. A great scholar who smiled on hearing of his son's death illustrates that contentment. The benefits are freedom from relying on your deeds, from resentment against Allah, the union of ambition and acceptance, courage to do what is right, and never feeling forgotten. Finally, of the four possible pairings of effort and outcome, the person of tawakkul sees good as Allah's gift and bad as a cause for self-review.

outline.heading: Opening
Foundations before spiritual states
outline.gist: Tears and feelings of closeness cannot be discussed until basic concepts are clear, so he mixes the order to keep it from becoming dry.

outline.heading: The companions' clarity came first
outline.gist: Self-worth, compassion and mortality were what the Meccan years taught, which let the companions reach their milestones.

outline.heading: Why emotional reminders alone fail
outline.gist: Stories of Paradise and Hell give a superficial, short-lived high when fundamentals are missing; revisit these sessions until they are clear.

outline.heading: Tawakkul links belief to practice
outline.gist: The Prophet's occasional reminders sufficed because people had clear fundamentals; tawakkul is the result of clarity on the pillars of faith.

outline.heading: We do not know what is best for us
outline.gist: You may hate what is good for you and love what is bad; our job is to assess, ask Allah and work towards it.

outline.heading: The 'who knows' tale of the farmer
outline.gist: Runaway horses, a stallion, a broken arm and a son spared from conscription show every culture knows we cannot judge outcomes.

outline.heading: Nothing arrives labelled: you hold the labelling gun
outline.gist: Wealth or illness becomes blessing or ruin by how you respond; no one can tell you a hardship is Allah's wrath.

outline.heading: Hardships are tax-free
outline.gist: Blessings carry a debt of gratitude before any reward; hardship met with patience owes nothing, and assuming Allah hates you is how Shaytan enters.

outline.heading: What you can and cannot control
outline.gist: Where you have no influence, the effort component falls away; tawakkul is the one act linking the unseen decree to the seen world.

outline.heading: Component one: doing your best
outline.gist: Without real effort you may ask Allah for a good outcome but cannot call it tawakkul; otherwise it becomes a numbing agent for passivity.

outline.heading: The exam example
outline.gist: If you did not study you cannot claim tawakkul for the exam, though no one's effort is ever flawless.

outline.heading: Component two: depending on Allah for the outcome
outline.gist: Even with the material mastered, illness, sleeplessness, an accident or a misread question can still cause failure.

outline.heading: Entrusting your affairs to One who never neglects
outline.gist: A person may forget your case; Allah is fully aware and has a plan for you.

outline.heading: Component three: contentment with the decree, not with yourself
outline.gist: You keep holding yourself accountable for your effort while accepting whatever Allah delivers.

outline.heading: Contentment as gratitude and perseverance
outline.gist: Perseverance in hardship is a simple act of acceptance; gratitude for blessings is harder because you never know if it was enough.

outline.heading: The scholar who smiled at his son's death
outline.gist: A stern worshipper of the two sanctuaries smiled on hearing his eldest son died, to show his contentment; scholars judged that weeping would also have been fine.

outline.heading: Benefit one: freedom from depending on your deeds
outline.gist: Relying on deeds for self-worth or Paradise breaks you when deeds falter; depend on Allah, whom our deeds do not benefit.

outline.heading: Benefit two: freedom from resentment against the decree
outline.gist: Objecting to what Allah sends is in essence an act of disbelief; tawakkul gives immunity from it.

outline.heading: Benefit three: ambition and acceptance together
outline.gist: Contentment does not mean lacking aspiration; it lets you accept an outcome and take the next step.

outline.heading: Benefit four: courage to do what pleases Allah
outline.gist: Knowing your affairs are in His hands lets you take a frightening but right stance; Muslims should not live in cowardice.

outline.heading: Benefit five: never feeling forgotten
outline.gist: When revelation paused, the Prophet was told his Lord had not abandoned him; hardship means testing, not neglect.

outline.heading: The four outcomes of decree
outline.gist: Ease or hardship, each arriving as the logical result of your effort or against it, give four combinations.

outline.heading: Seeing only two: good from Allah, bad as self-review
outline.gist: The person of tawakkul never credits himself for good or blames Allah for bad; good is a gift, and bad prompts accountability and new plans.

outline.heading: Tawakkul as immunity and a Muslim's distinct worldview
outline.gist: It produces gratitude in ease, perseverance in hardship and courage to stand by the truth; without it you cannot function as a Muslim.

St27fU4_nnI.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 11: Compassion (Rahma)
St27fU4_nnI.one_line: Rahma as a baseline owed to every creature without exception, its bond with humbleness, and its three steps: perspective, feeling and treatment.
St27fU4_nnI.summary: He calls rahma the defining Islamic attitude and the very essence of the Prophet. It is a sensitive test of faith: if learning the religion leaves you with less mercy, you are learning it wrong. Every creature is owed a baseline of mercy that a Muslim never drops below, whatever others do; you may go above it for those you love. He links this to Allah's names ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim. Even punishments carry mercy in how they are carried out, and sometimes mercy to the community outweighs leniency to the individual, as when the Prophet forbade cursing a man being lashed for drinking. You may not love an enemy or forgive a betrayal, but excluding anyone from mercy turns it into selective tenderness, which even tyrants have. Since no deed earns Paradise, we all depend on Allah's mercy. He describes a triangle: love needs both humbleness and rahma, and each of those collapses without the other; mercy without humbleness becomes pity. Rahma has three steps: put yourself in another's place, never claiming you could not have done what they did; feel what they feel, as fasting teaches; and treat them as you would want to be treated, which can include strictness. He closes with the Prophet weeping for his ummah and protecting a mother dog on the march to Mecca.

outline.heading: Opening
Rahma as the partner of humbleness
outline.gist: Rahma is inseparable from humbleness; without one the other fails.

outline.heading: Rahma: the Islamic attitude and the Prophet's essence
outline.gist: Everything deserves baseline mercy; Allah described the Prophet himself as a mercy, making rahma the most sensitive test of Islam.

outline.heading: More knowledge must mean more mercy
outline.gist: Mercy grows with closeness to Allah; if your learning leaves you harsher, you are being taught wrongly.

outline.heading: Never dipping below the baseline
outline.gist: A Muslim does not drop below baseline mercy even when others do, and there can be no exceptions for a dictator or an ex-spouse.

outline.heading: Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim: baseline and extra mercy
outline.gist: One name is the mercy owed to all creation, the other the added mercy for those who believe; you may rise above the baseline but not fall below.

outline.heading: Mercy inside punishment: the individual and the collective
outline.gist: Even severe punishments are carried out with mercy, and their harshness is mercy to the community and future generations.

outline.heading: The man lashed for drinking
outline.gist: When a companion cursed him during the punishment, the Prophet forbade it, saying the man loved Allah and His Messenger.

outline.heading: You need not love an enemy, but must show mercy
outline.gist: You may not forgive, stay friends or stay married, yet empathy and compassion remain possible for everyone.

outline.heading: Selective tenderness is not rahma
outline.gist: Tyrants and Shaytan show tenderness to some; mercy only counts if it covers everyone.

outline.heading: All we can hope for is Allah's mercy
outline.gist: Nothing we do can equal eternity in Paradise; the goal of life is to be found worthy of His mercy.

outline.heading: The man who would enter Paradise by his deeds
outline.gist: His lifetime of worship did not outweigh a single blessing; no one enters by deeds, not even the Prophet, except by Allah's mercy.

outline.heading: Mercy within strictness
outline.gist: Making a child sleep early, go to school and eat well is mercy; rahma does not mean letting people walk over you.

outline.heading: Gentleness beautifies everything
outline.gist: The Prophet kept a dose of mercy even with enemies and traitors because it was his value, not their due; a dictator is punished, still with mercy.

outline.heading: The triangle: love rests on humbleness and rahma
outline.gist: Without them love turns narcissistic and controlling, as seen when former lovers try to destroy each other in court.

outline.heading: Humbleness and rahma cannot exist without each other
outline.gist: Humbleness needs mercy to see others as equal or better; mercy needs humbleness to step into another's shoes, or it becomes sympathy.

outline.heading: Pity: mercy mutated by the lack of humbleness
outline.gist: People reject pity because it looks down on them; when both virtues exist they produce love, the goal of Ramadan.

outline.heading: Step one: putting yourself in their place
outline.gist: From the hadith on loving for your brother what you love for yourself, the hardest step needs humbleness.

outline.heading: Never say 'I would never do that'
outline.gist: Claiming you could not fall into someone's sin is almost a challenge to Allah.

outline.heading: Trading Places: anyone's life can be overturned
outline.gist: In the film two rich men swap a CEO and a homeless man for a bet; if people can do that, Allah certainly can, so the Quran's stories are for us.

outline.heading: We stand only because we have not been pushed far enough
outline.gist: Everyone has a breaking point; praise Allah for concealing our weaknesses, and read the stories of past nations as warnings for ourselves.

outline.heading: The homeless man in a land of opportunity
outline.gist: You need not give, but do not condescend; you do not know what led someone to that point.

outline.heading: Step two: feeling their pain, as fasting teaches
outline.gist: Understanding is not excusing the wrong; hunger and fatigue in fasting let you feel others' suffering.

outline.heading: Step three: treat them as you would want to be treated
outline.gist: That may mean real help or even strictness that helps them grow, rather than a handout, but always within mercy.

outline.heading: The first hadith every student hears
outline.gist: The narration that the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful is traditionally taught first, each teacher saying it was the first he heard.

outline.heading: The Prophet weeping for his ummah
outline.gist: Repeating the verse 'if You punish them, they are Your servants' all night, he was told Allah would please him regarding his nation.

outline.heading: Guarding a mother dog on the march to Mecca
outline.gist: The Prophet posted a man to protect a nursing dog until the whole army had passed.

outline.heading: Mercy for everyone except the ex-spouse
outline.gist: People show mercy to all but their former spouse; if one person is unworthy of mercy, you only have selective tenderness.

EVm8wiNEgr0.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 14: Quranic Themes, Correct Attitudes
EVm8wiNEgr0.one_line: The Quran corrects attitudes: dawah with wisdom, tender reminders and kind argument (16:125), saying what is best (17:53), and the Prophet's sorrow for those who rejected him (18:6).
EVm8wiNEgr0.summary: He opens by reminding listeners that the Quran is not a history, geography or science book but a book of law, wisdom, psychology and priorities, so time spent mining it for other things is wasted. One of its major themes is attitude: how a Muslim carries himself toward people, life and Allah. A survey of American Muslims found religious people to be the main reason others are repelled from Islam, and he blames attitude, not knowledge: harshness, shouting and disrespect in the masjid. Employers and suitors' fathers look for attitude above credentials, and harshness belongs only to the battlefield. From 16:125 he separates dawah, the task, from attitude, the manner: wisdom drawn from those who did it well, tender emotional reminders that loosen hardened hearts, and argument in the best way to help people see rather than to win, since Allah alone knows who is guided. Two stories of harsh worshippers driving seekers away illustrate the cost. From 17:53 he urges pausing to find the best thing to say, because words cannot be retrieved and Shaytan exploits ambiguity to sow enmity. From 18:6 he describes the Prophet grieving over those who refused to believe, explains asaf as the only true apology, and closes with his prayer for his people's forgiveness.

outline.heading: The Quran is not a history book
outline.gist: It tells stories from history, but its goal was never to document events or give the Arabs information they lacked.

outline.heading: Why the Arabs' local knowledge was lost
outline.gist: Mass migrations out of Arabia, from Spain to India, and newcomers settling near the Kaaba, erased knowledge of places the first audience took for granted.

outline.heading: Read the Quran for what it came to teach
outline.gist: It is a book of law, sociology, psychology and wisdom; searching it for science it was not revealed to teach wastes effort we need for the basics.

outline.heading: What attitudes cover
outline.gist: Roughness or gentleness, pessimism or optimism, good or bad assumptions about others; the Quran keeps correcting these because a wrong attitude derails everything.

outline.heading: Religious people as the main repeller
outline.gist: A survey of about 600 American Muslims found people who claim religiosity to be by far the top reason others turn from Islam, and the cause is attitude, not ideas.

outline.heading: Bad attitudes in the masjid
outline.gist: Screaming, pushing past people at the doors and chatting during a talk all show a lack of respect and empathy.

outline.heading: Testing a suitor's attitude
outline.gist: Good attitude is not being a doormat; in Sham a father may provoke a suitor to see his temper, because attitude governs every relationship.

outline.heading: Employers hire attitude, not resumes
outline.gist: Mentors and employers look for professionalism, care and enthusiasm; knowledge can be taught, a bad attitude ruins a workplace.

outline.heading: Harshness belongs to the battlefield
outline.gist: Harshness toward anyone, practising or not, has almost no place in a Muslim's attitude outside war.

outline.heading: Call to the way of your Lord
outline.gist: Anyone fully committed to the deen will invite others to it, the mission of the prophets, whether helping Muslims or reaching non-Muslims.

outline.heading: Dawah is the what, attitude is the how
outline.gist: Your job title or noble work matters less than how you do it, and the verse specifies the how.

outline.heading: Wisdom: learning from those before you
outline.gist: Hikmah is an attitude of relying on what worked for others, applying it, refining it and passing it on.

outline.heading: Accountable for winging it
outline.gist: Reinventing the wheel earns no extra reward, and you answer for pushing people away when wisdom was available.

outline.heading: The worshipper and the scholar
outline.gist: A man who wanted to learn to pray was screamed at by a worshipper; a scholar taught him gently, then brought him back to show the worshipper what he had nearly lost.

outline.heading: Tender emotional reminders
outline.gist: Al-maw'izah al-hasanah is a kind reminder that shakes the clay from a heart hardened by materialism.

outline.heading: Argue in the best way
outline.gist: Respond to objections in the kindest, most correct way, aiming to help people see, not to prove them wrong.

outline.heading: Allah knows who is guided
outline.gist: Judging others is not your job; Allah is worshipped the way He wants, so His call must be carried out the way He wants.

outline.heading: The young man and the shisha café
outline.gist: Scolded for his clothes and wudu, a young man left the masjid for a café whose owner shrugged off a broken pipe, and returned there daily; religiosity must not make us harsh and condescending.

outline.heading: Say what is best
outline.gist: Say what best serves the person in front of you, not your ego; words once spoken can never be taken back, making the tongue the most dangerous organ.

outline.heading: Hold your tongue
outline.gist: The Prophet took hold of his own tongue to warn a companion that what people say casts them into the Fire more than anything else.

outline.heading: Dominate, or say what is best?
outline.gist: Everyone loses their temper at times; the question is whether you aim to outsmart and correct or to say what is best in Allah's sight.

outline.heading: Pause and you will know
outline.gist: Stopping for a second in any argument, especially with a spouse, reveals the best thing to say even if ego stops you saying it.

outline.heading: Shaytan sows discord through ambiguity
outline.gist: Words that are not wrong but open to a bad reading let Shaytan build enmity out of nothing and tear apart brotherhood.

outline.heading: Your Lord knows you best
outline.gist: You are not responsible for people; whether Allah treats you with mercy depends on what you chose to say.

outline.heading: Say it for them, not for you
outline.gist: Choose words and tone so you cannot be misunderstood; correct people to bring them closer to Allah, not to feel superior.

outline.heading: What would Allah want me to say?
outline.gist: The answer is always easy; the real question is whether you will put your ego aside.

outline.heading: Would you destroy yourself over them?
outline.gist: Allah twice tells the Prophet he may harm himself psychologically out of care for those he called.

outline.heading: Grief over those who would not believe
outline.gist: When Abu Jahl and Abu Sufyan would not respond, he saw himself as failing them and lost sleep and joy.

outline.heading: The word placed at the end
outline.gist: Asafa is moved to the end of the verse for emphasis, the same word Ya'qub used when grief for Yusuf blinded him.

outline.heading: Asaf as the true apology
outline.gist: Asaf means being in pain over the hurt you caused someone, which is the only real apology.

outline.heading: Sorry you feel that way is no apology
outline.gist: Own what you did rather than commenting on another person's feelings.

outline.heading: The Prophet's sorrow for them
outline.gist: He spent nights in dua and tears for those who would not believe; Allah told him to do his job but not to destroy himself.

outline.heading: Forgive my people, they do not know
outline.gist: Even when they wounded him and killed his uncle he prayed for their forgiveness; that is the attitude to learn.

5Or-x5Yd2_8.title: Ramadan 2025 Night 21: Proper Representations
5Or-x5Yd2_8.one_line: Because Islam is judged by its followers, Muslims must represent it well: in the home, in hijab, in unpaid religious leadership and in carrying the Quran.
5Or-x5Yd2_8.summary: He argues that while Muslims judge a faith by its teachings, others judge Islam by how Muslims behave, so believers hold themselves to two standards in order to bring hearts to Allah. Imams, parents and volunteers carry this most: children normalise what they see at home and are repelled by hypocrisy, and those serving in the masjid must be gentle or step aside. From 33:59 he explains that the outer garment lets Muslim women be recognised and not harmed; their dress is the most visible representation of Islam, the Prophet addresses them directly without a sheikh as middleman, and Allah knows the courage hijab requires in the West. From 34:47, where every prophet says he asks no wage, he makes a long case against monetising religion: his teachers in Syria all had professions, the classical imams paid their students, and paying imams turns leaders into employees fired by boards and cheapens knowledge. He wants future imams to build careers and serve independently. From 35:32 he describes the Quran as the Prophet's only inheritance and the three kinds of people who receive it, urging listeners to be foremost in good with it, the one thing besides generous wealth worth envying.

outline.heading: The last ten nights
outline.gist: Scholars resolved the question of the best times by naming the first ten days of Dhul Hijjah the best days and the last ten nights of Ramadan the best nights; they can make up for earlier neglect.

outline.heading: Interlude
Representing Islam is a requirement
outline.gist: The theme runs through the Sunnah and underlies juristic rulings: faiths and groups are judged by their followers' behaviour, which is wrong but real.

outline.heading: Two standards for the sake of hearts
outline.gist: Muslims judge by teachings, not people, yet behave knowing others will judge Islam by them, since the goal is to bring hearts closer to Allah.

outline.heading: Imams and the Prophet held to a higher standard
outline.gist: Whoever takes the minbar accepts that his mistakes are magnified; if you cannot bear that, stay on the other side.

outline.heading: Parents represent what is normal
outline.gist: Children normalise whatever their parents do; yelling and abuse at home harms their future relationships and self-worth.

outline.heading: Children sniff out hypocrisy
outline.gist: Picking and choosing from Islam teaches hypocrisy and repels children; many youth he counsels carry damage from senseless rules and bad practice that a short session cannot undo.

outline.heading: Volunteers must represent with tenderness
outline.gist: Those serving cannot yell at or mistreat people; without the patience to welcome them, this work is not for you.

outline.heading: The outer garment for believing women
outline.gist: The jilbab covers without showing the figure, so women represent Islam and their adherence to it and are not harmed or misjudged.

outline.heading: Why this verse addresses women
outline.gist: People should not judge by dress but will; a man's faith may be guessed, a woman in hijab is unmistakable, so her obligation and reward are greater.

outline.heading: Women set the public norm
outline.gist: Women's dress shapes the communal standard in a way men's does not, reflecting natural differences in how bodies are seen.

outline.heading: No middleman: the Prophet speaks to the sisters
outline.gist: The command starts with his wives and daughters, setting their standard; women can judge for themselves what is revealing without asking a sheikh.

outline.heading: Known and not harmed: the courage of hijab in the West
outline.gist: Allah knows the bravery it takes for a minority woman to dress differently; he prays for their strength and warns against a culture pushing to unveil everything.

outline.heading: Every prophet: 'I ask you no wage'
outline.gist: Among a series of 'say' commands, the Prophet repeats what every prophet said: any payment is yours, my reward is with Allah.

outline.heading: Islam is not a business
outline.gist: Monetising the deen removes its barakah; prophets with no time for a job still refused pay, and the Prophet spent and pawned his own belongings for others.

outline.heading: His teachers in Syria all had professions
outline.gist: Physicians, engineers and merchants who took nothing; one coppersmith would don his robe and step out like Superman as the region's imam.

outline.heading: Paid imams become employees
outline.gist: Endowment ministries and salaried imams, though permissible, misrepresent the deen; he has never seen anyone pay a person and still respect him as a leader.

outline.heading: The classical imams took nothing
outline.gist: Abu Hanifah was a merchant who supported Abu Yusuf; al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Malik refused state money, preserving the integrity of Islamic law.

outline.heading: No price equals knowledge
outline.gist: Forty dollars cannot equal what a child learns of the Quran, which is why everything at the centre is free; seekers come to receive, not to hire.

outline.heading: Imams with their own careers, not hired by boards
outline.gist: The next generation should have professions and give dawah independently rather than be told what to say by elected boards; Muslim Wellness Network was built on this model.

outline.heading: Cheapening sacred knowledge in Syria
outline.gist: Students who gained admission nowhere else were placed in sharia faculties by default, so the least accomplished became the voices of the faith.

outline.heading: Masjid funds serve the community, not the imam
outline.gist: Expansion is for the people's next generation; most workers are volunteers, with two or three hires only for roles volunteers cannot cover.

outline.heading: Restoring respect for the minbar
outline.gist: It is disgraceful that an imam must fear being fired and unable to feed his children; he urges imams to build careers and serve from conviction.

outline.heading: His father's gift to his teacher
outline.gist: His sheikh nearly ended the lessons over a small thank-you gift, because attaching money teaches the mind that knowledge has a price.

outline.heading: The Book as the inheritance
outline.gist: Allah passed the Book down to those He chose; the prophets left knowledge, not gold or silver.

outline.heading: The Prophet left nothing to inherit
outline.gist: His shield was pawned and only sentimental relics remained, some still kept by scholars he used to visit.

outline.heading: Those who inherit the Book must represent it
outline.gist: Like the sisters and the Prophet, those given the Quran either represent it well or they do not.

outline.heading: Those who wrong themselves with it
outline.gist: They learn what the Quran teaches, then practise the opposite while putting on a show.

outline.heading: Like the one who cast off Allah's signs
outline.gist: Given the verses as a beautiful covering, he threw it off and clung to the earth like a panting dog; you will tire either way, so tire for the right reason.

outline.heading: The reciter who learned for show
outline.gist: Among the first used to kindle the Fire is one who learned the Quran to be admired; he got what he sought and is owed nothing.

outline.heading: The moderate and those foremost in good
outline.gist: Some do just enough, barely breaking even; others race ahead applying and spreading the Book, which is the great bounty.

outline.heading: Envy permitted only in two things
outline.gist: Do not waste desire on cars or houses; only the one who lives and teaches the Quran and the one who spends wealth for Allah are worth envying. He closes asking to be among the people of the Quran.
