WyjxQZBddbQ.title: Tazkiyah Pearls 10: Principles and Tools of Tazkiyah
WyjxQZBddbQ.one_line: A reference session on the four principles of striving against the self and the external, internal, lifestyle and reinforcement methods of tazkiyah.
WyjxQZBddbQ.summary: He frames the session as a reference to revisit. Starting from the Prophet's fear that his ummah would obey greed, follow desire and admire their own opinions, he explains the verse about taking one's desire as a god, and draws a second reading: people can reshape their very image of Allah to suit what they want. Striving against the self rests on four principles. Change must be gradual and gentle, because the self adapts but can break, and overnight transformations rebound. You need raw honesty with yourself and Allah even while keeping a social face, since nothing can be treated in denial. Small habits must be completely consistent, as Ali kept his bedtime dhikr even on a night of battle. And a sin must be left completely, with something good substituted to fill the gap. He then groups the methods. External: knowledge to feed new thoughts into the cycle of thought, feeling and action; good companions; mentors who teach by how they live; and a supportive environment. Internal: contemplation and exercises such as doing a disliked act of service daily until the self stops resisting. Lifestyle: sleep on the Prophet's pattern, not filling the stomach, a steady routine and physical health. Reinforcement: dhikr, dua and the Quran. He asks listeners to take what benefits them and apply it.

outline.heading: A reference session on the basics of tazkiyah
outline.gist: The material is dense and meant to be revisited; he is summarising a third of Islam in a short series.

outline.heading: What the Prophet feared most for his ummah
outline.gist: Obeyed greed, followed desire and vanity in one's own opinion, all diseases of the inner self.

outline.heading: Taking one's desire as a god
outline.gist: The self rarely wants anything for a good reason, so some scholars had beginners simply oppose their desires for years.

outline.heading: Shaping Allah to fit our desires
outline.gist: The verse also warns of distorting one's image of Allah; the angry want a god of wrath, the weak a god of endless mercy, but He is who He is.

outline.heading: Striving against the self: principles and methods
outline.gist: The self thinks it knows what is best but does not; he will give four principles and four methods of striving.

outline.heading: Principle one: gradual and gentle change
outline.gist: The self is remarkably adaptable, but flexibility does not mean it cannot be broken by trauma.

outline.heading: Harshness breaks the self, as with children
outline.gist: Treating children too harshly can cause lifelong damage; the aim of tazkiyah is to reshape the self, not destroy it.

outline.heading: Why overnight transformations rebound
outline.gist: Someone who goes from no prayer to every sunnah at once usually collapses; extreme change needs extreme circumstances.

outline.heading: Principle two: honesty and self-transparency
outline.gist: If you rationalise your habits or think yourself better than you are, nothing changes; some scholars put this first.

outline.heading: A social mask for people, raw honesty before Allah
outline.gist: Concealing sins from others is right, but you must face yourself without the persona; like a patient in denial, you cannot be treated otherwise.

outline.heading: Closing the door on the messy room
outline.gist: People avoid looking inside because the mess feels overwhelming, then deny how far behind they are.

outline.heading: Principle three: small, consistent habits
outline.gist: The deeds most beloved to Allah are consistent even if small, such as daily dhikr and a little Quran.

outline.heading: Ali's bedtime dhikr, even on the night of battle
outline.gist: Taught the bedtime tasbih by the Prophet, Ali never missed it, in any condition.

outline.heading: Making daily reflection a fixed habit
outline.gist: Habits you add, like ten to fifteen minutes of deep thought each day, must be self-driven and constant.

outline.heading: Principle four: complete abstinence
outline.gist: As in recovery from alcohol, leaving a sin means cutting off everything associated with it.

outline.heading: Substitution fills the gap
outline.gist: Leaving a habit leaves a void; without something fulfilling in its place you rebound, as many do after Ramadan.

outline.heading: The principles recapped: treat the self like a child
outline.gist: Gentleness, honest courage that also breeds humbleness, resetting broken habits, and stopping cold turkey except for addictions needing supervision.

outline.heading: Four categories of method and the cycle of thought, feeling and action
outline.gist: Negative feelings, thoughts and deeds feed each other in a vicious cycle that an outside force can break.

outline.heading: External method: knowledge
outline.gist: New information gives contemplation fresh material and turns the cycle virtuous; inner effort fails without outside teaching.

outline.heading: External method: companionship
outline.gist: Your time and attention are your most valuable assets; bad friends undo everything at any age, so keep company that draws you closer to Allah.

outline.heading: External method: mentorship
outline.gist: The path is walked with someone who has walked it; Allah sent a Prophet with the Book, beginning a chain of teachers.

outline.heading: A week with a teacher who barely ate or slept
outline.gist: He recalls struggling to keep up with a late teacher; observing such a life stays with you.

outline.heading: External method: environment
outline.gist: Where you spend your time shapes you, in religion and in any craft, such as becoming a good doctor.

outline.heading: Internal method: contemplation
outline.gist: Deep thought on important topics changes how you feel and act.

outline.heading: Internal method: exercises against the self
outline.gist: Do a disliked act of service every day until the self stops resisting, so you learn to recognise its pushback.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: sleep on the Prophet's pattern
outline.gist: Tazkiyah fails without good sleep; the Prophet slept early, rose for prayer and napped by day, as did his own teachers.

outline.heading: Resetting the routine: camps near Damascus and army service
outline.gist: Summer tazkiyah camps without electricity, and compulsory army service at university, reset his broken routine; camping can do the same for families.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: never filling the stomach
outline.gist: Muslims follow everything except the hadith on thirds of the stomach; healthy eating is part of the path.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: a steady daily routine
outline.gist: Structure is healthy, not boring; psychiatrists prescribe routine against depression.

outline.heading: Lifestyle: physical health and the heart
outline.gist: Spiritual terms are named after body parts for a reason; a neglected body will not carry a healthy spiritual heart.

outline.heading: Reinforcement: dhikr, dua and Quran
outline.gist: Specific words of remembrance counter vanity and arrogance; reciting Quran, hadith and stories reinforces every concept.

93Ma0f6bKDs.title: Ramadan 2025, Night 21: First Night of Tahajjud
93Ma0f6bKDs.one_line: Opening a series on the movements of the prayer: the standing as a dialogue with Allah, the Prophet's long recitation, and bowing.
93Ma0f6bKDs.summary: On the twenty-first night of Ramadan 2025 the sheikh begins a series for the last ten nights on the movements of the prayer. We do not pray in a single posture, he says, because each movement is meant to do something different to the soul. In the first reminder he takes the standing. It is the longest part of the best prayer, and in it we recite Allah's words back to Him, memorized word for word, with reflection and love. He explains the hadith qudsi in which Allah answers each verse of Al-Fatiha, tells how Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz paused after every verse to imagine his Lord's reply, and teaches that Allah faces the worshipper for as long as the worshipper faces Him, turning away once something else matters more in the heart. In the second reminder he shows how the Prophet and his companions found joy in the standing: Ibn Mas'ud's recitation of An-Nisa that brought the Prophet to tears, and the night prayer in which the Prophet recited Al-Baqarah, An-Nisa and Aal-Imran in one rakah, pausing to ask for Paradise and refuge from the Fire. He then turns to bowing, which once meant taking a knee before someone greater, and to the words of glorification and surrender said in it.

outline.heading: Interlude
These nights are for the prayer itself
outline.gist: He sets the prayer itself as the subject of his reminders on these nights, since nothing is more worth talking about while standing in it.

outline.heading: Each movement mirrors a change in the spirit
outline.gist: We do not pray in one posture; we stand, bow, rise, prostrate and sit because each movement is meant to do something different inside us, bringing humility and clarity.

outline.heading: Standing: reciting His words back to Him
outline.gist: The best prayer is the one with the longest standing; in it we show that we have not only accepted and applied His revelation but memorized it word for word and recite it back to Him with reflection and love.

outline.heading: Allah answers each verse of Al-Fatiha
outline.gist: In the hadith qudsi Allah divides the prayer between Himself and His servant: He replies 'My servant has praised Me', 'has glorified Me', 'this is between Me and My servant', and 'My servant shall have what he asked'.

outline.heading: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz waits for the answer
outline.gist: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz paused after each verse of Al-Fatiha; asked why, he said he was picturing his Lord's reply.

outline.heading: He faces you as long as you face Him
outline.gist: Allah faces the servant who stands in prayer and responds as he speaks; the moment something else becomes more important in the heart, Allah turns away, but as long as you are focused on Him He is focused on you.

outline.heading: When the heart overflows, the tongue stumbles
outline.gist: He closes with something he has witnessed over twenty-five years: so much can come onto a worshipper's heart in the standing that his tongue stumbles from its abundance.

outline.heading: Interlude
The standing, the movement most worth contemplating
outline.gist: He returns to the standing as the part of the prayer he considers most worthy of reflection.

outline.heading: Ibn Mas'ud joins the Prophet's night prayer
outline.gist: The Prophet and companions found such joy in standing that their stories make it seem all they did; Ibn Mas'ud found the Prophet praying alone one night, joined him expecting a short prayer, and heard him begin Al-Baqarah.

outline.heading: The verse that made the Prophet weep
outline.gist: When Ibn Mas'ud recited An-Nisa to him and reached the verse about bringing a witness from every nation, the Prophet told him to stop, his eyes flowing with tears.

outline.heading: A hundred verses, then past them
outline.gist: In one rakah the Prophet went past a hundred verses, finished Al-Baqarah, then recited An-Nisa and Aal-Imran, until his companion was tempted to sit down and leave him.

outline.heading: Pausing at Paradise and the Fire
outline.gist: He recited unhurriedly, stopping at a mention of the Fire to seek refuge and at a mention of Paradise to ask for it, living the Quran as he prayed.

outline.heading: Bowing: taking the knee
outline.gist: Bowing was long the sign of admitting someone's superiority; taking the knee means accepting that the one before you is greater and that you are not his equal.

outline.heading: What is said in ruku
outline.gist: Ruku is for magnifying the Lord with the Prophet's words, such as glorifying the Lord of the angels and the Spirit and the dua offering one's hearing, sight, mind and bones in submission.

outline.heading: Interlude
Outro

hadith.gist: The best prayer is the one with the longest standing.
Hadith qudsi: Allah has divided the prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each verse of Al-Fatiha; His servant shall have what he asks.
Allah keeps facing His servant in prayer as long as he does not turn away; when he turns away, Allah turns away from him.
When the servant stands in prayer, Allah faces him.
Ibn Mas'ud joined the Prophet's night prayer, which was so long that he was tempted to sit down and leave him.
Ibn Mas'ud recited An-Nisa to the Prophet, who said he loved to hear it from another; at the verse of the witness he said 'enough' with tears flowing.
In one rakah the Prophet recited Al-Baqarah, An-Nisa and Aal-Imran slowly, asking for Paradise and seeking refuge from the Fire when they were mentioned.
As for ruku, magnify the Lord in it; the Prophet's words in ruku include glorifying the Lord of the angels and the Spirit, and the Lord of might, dominion, grandeur and majesty.

takeaways: Treat each movement of the prayer as a distinct inner act, not a routine posture.
Pause after each verse of Al-Fatiha and remember that Allah is answering you.
Keep your heart on Allah in prayer, knowing He turns away when you turn to something else.
Recite slowly in night prayer, asking for Paradise and refuge from the Fire when they come up.
Bow as an admission that Allah is greater, using the Prophet's words of glorification in ruku.
